title: Own price elasticity and total revenue
summary: Own price elasticity, elastic, inelastic and unitary demand, the two extreme cases, and what a price change does to total revenue.

chunks.heading: Own price elasticity of demand
chunks.explanation_md:
**Own price elasticity** measures how quantity demanded of good X responds to a change in the price of X itself:

**E(QX,PX) = %ΔQd / %ΔPX**

By the **law of demand** it is **negative** (price up, quantity down). To classify demand look at the **absolute value**:

- **Elastic**: |E| > 1
- **Inelastic**: |E| < 1
- **Unitary**: |E| = 1

chunks.heading: Own price elasticity and total revenue
chunks.explanation_md:
What happens to **total revenue** when price changes depends on elasticity:

- **Elastic demand**: a price **increase** lowers total revenue; a price **decrease** raises it.
- **Inelastic demand**: a price **increase** raises total revenue; a price **decrease** lowers it.
- **Unitary demand**: total revenue is **maximized** where demand is unitary elastic.

This is the **total revenue test**, the same idea as the total expenditure method of finding elasticity: watch what happens to price and total revenue (price times quantity) together.

key_terms.meaning: Price times quantity, TR = P × Q.

chunks.exam_line: Elastic: price and TR move in opposite directions. Inelastic: price and TR move the same way. TR is maximized at unitary elasticity.

questions.stem: Explain how the elasticity of demand decides what happens to total revenue when the price is lowered.
questions.model_answer_md:
A price cut changes revenue in different ways depending on elasticity.

- **Elastic demand**: a price decrease **raises** total revenue.
- **Inelastic demand**: a price decrease **lowers** total revenue.
- **Unitary demand**: total revenue is at its **maximum**.

So a firm facing elastic demand gains by cutting price.

questions.stem: Differentiate between elastic and inelastic demand.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Point | Elastic | Inelastic |
|---|---|---|
| Elasticity | \|E\| > 1 | \|E\| < 1 |
| Price rise | Total revenue falls | Total revenue rises |
| Price fall | Total revenue rises | Total revenue falls |

In short, elastic demand responds strongly to price; inelastic demand responds weakly.

questions.stem: Explain own price elasticity of demand and the relationship between price, elasticity and total revenue.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** Own price elasticity of demand shows how sensitive quantity demanded of a good is to its own price.

**Formula.** E = %Δ quantity demanded / %ΔPX, negative by the law of demand.

**Cases.**
- Elastic |E| > 1
- Inelastic |E| < 1
- Unitary |E| = 1
- Extremes: perfectly elastic (infinite) and perfectly inelastic (0).

**Total revenue.**
- Elastic: price up, TR down; price down, TR up.
- Inelastic: price up, TR up; price down, TR down.
- Unitary: TR is maximized.

**Conclusion.** A manager who knows elasticity can predict whether a price change will raise or lower revenue.

rubric.point: Inelastic TR rule and TR maximized at unitary

questions.stem: For a firm, a price change moves revenue up in some cases and down in others. Explain why, covering elastic, inelastic and unitary demand.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** What a price change does to revenue depends on how strongly quantity demanded reacts.

**Elastic (|E| > 1).** Quantity changes by a bigger percentage than price, so price and total revenue move in opposite directions.

**Inelastic (|E| < 1).** Quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price, so price and total revenue move in the same direction.

**Unitary (|E| = 1).** Total revenue is maximized at the point where demand is unitary elastic.

**Conclusion.** Check elasticity before raising or cutting a price.
